newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY BANKS, BROKERS SET FOR SHAKEUP - EX-CENBANKER.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY BANKS, BROKERS SET FOR SHAKEUP - EX-CENBANKER.

text.p: Hungary has too many small banks and brokerages, and their numbers are bound to be thinned in the next few years, the former vice president of the Hungarian central bank said on Friday.

"For the size of the country, the 46 commercial banks we have today is just too many," Sandor Czirjak, who left the National Bank of Hungary late last year, told a professional conference. "As Hungarian banking clients are becoming more sophisticated, they realise that one way to reduce risks is to deal with better capitalised, larger institutions."
All but about a half a dozen Hungarian commercial banks are small by local standards. A few are state-owned, but most have local or foreign private owners.
Czirjak said that a similar shakeup is likely among brokerages, which include many that are simply too small to handle the increasing volume of trade on the Budapest Stock Exchange.
Daily turnover on the exchange has increased to two to four billion forints a day compared to some 100-200 million about two years ago.
"When the Stock Exchange was set up (in 1990), it was like a cooperative, with everybody being equal," he said. "But now people don't want to deal with mom-and-pop shops."
The Stock Exchange had 56 members, plus the central bank, at the end of December.
For commercial banks, the way to ensure survival would be to improve their retail services and improve cooperation with their insurance and brokerage subsidiaries, Czirjak said.
Peter Kazar, senior manager at Ernst & Young's local unit, echoed Czirjak's statements, saying that Hungarian banks are too dependent on mid-sized corporations for their profits.

"Companies realise that they do not have to have all their accounts at one bank, so competition for these accounts is bound to become stronger," he told the conference. "Banks must start making more money on retail banking if they are to survive."
Czirjak said that the situation will not be significantly changed after next year, when Hungary will permit foreign banks to open branches in the country without setting up local banks.
"Those foreign banks that want to be here are already here," he said.
